outputs.L1:
Tulsidas, the poet, wandered deep in thought along the Ganges, through that lonely place where the dead were burned. There he found a woman seated at the feet of her husband’s corpse, dressed gaily as though for a wedding.

When she saw him, she rose, bowed, and said, “Permit me, Master, with your blessing, to follow my husband to heaven.”

“Why such haste, my daughter?” asked Tulsidas. “Does not this earth also belong to Him who made heaven?”

“I do not long for heaven,” said the woman. “I want my husband.”

Tulsidas smiled and said to her, “Return to your home, my child. Before the month is over, you will find your husband.”

The woman returned home filled with joyful hope. Tulsidas visited her every day, giving her lofty thoughts to contemplate until her heart was filled to the brim with divine love.

When the month was scarcely over, her neighbours came to her and asked, “Woman, have you found your husband?”

The widow smiled and replied, “I have.”

“Where is he?” they asked eagerly.

“My lord is in my heart, one with me,” said the woman.
outputs.L2:
The poet Tulsidas was walking pensively along the Ganges when he reached a deserted cremation ground. There he noticed a woman adorned in festive bridal clothes, seated beside her husband’s lifeless body.

When she saw Tulsidas, she stood, bowed respectfully, and asked, “Master, give me your blessing and allow me to accompany my husband to heaven.”

“My daughter, why are you so eager to leave?” Tulsidas replied. “Does not the One who created heaven also possess this earth?”

“I have no desire for heaven,” she answered. “It is my husband whom I seek.”

Smiling, Tulsidas told her, “Return home, my child. You will find your husband before this month has ended.”

Filled with joyful expectation, the woman obeyed. Each day afterward, Tulsidas visited her and offered her noble ideas upon which to reflect. Gradually, divine love overflowed within her heart.

The month had barely passed when her neighbors approached and asked, “Have you found your husband?”

The widow smiled. “Yes, I have.”

“Where is he?” they demanded eagerly.

“My lord lives within my heart,” she replied. “He and I are one.”
outputs.L3:
Tulsidas once encountered a grieving widow by the banks of the Ganges. Believing that her dead husband had gone to heaven, she intended to follow him. Tulsidas gently questioned her haste, reminding her that both earth and heaven belong to the Divine and that there was no need to seek elsewhere what might be found within.

He assured the widow that she would find her husband within a month and encouraged her to return home. Trusting his words, she began attending Tulsidas’s daily teachings. As she listened, contemplated, and opened her heart to the Divine, her sorrow gradually changed. The grief that had consumed her was transformed into a deep and profound love of God.

At the end of the month, the widow returned to Tulsidas. With peace and joy, she declared that his promise had been fulfilled: she had found her husband within her own heart, inseparably united with her in divine love.
outputs.L4:
When a grieving widow prepared to follow her dead husband into death, the poet-saint Tulsidas intervened. He urged her not to act in the blindness of sorrow, explaining that death could not restore the companionship she had lost. Instead, he asked her to remain with him for one month and listen each day to spiritual teachings. If, after that time, she still believed that dying was the only way to reunite with her husband, she could reconsider her decision.

The widow agreed. Day after day, Tulsidas spoke to her about the soul, the impermanence of the body, and the love of God. He taught her that the deepest bonds between people do not depend solely on physical presence. Bodies appear and disappear, but genuine love leaves an enduring imprint on the heart. Through prayer, reflection, and devotion, grief can gradually be transformed from a force of destruction into a path toward spiritual understanding.

At first, the widow could think only of her loss. Her husband’s absence seemed to fill every part of her life. Yet as she continued listening, her sorrow began to change. She slowly understood that love was not confined to the body that had died. The memories, affection, and spiritual connection she shared with her husband remained alive within her.

By the end of the month, Tulsidas asked whether she still wished to follow her husband into death. The widow replied that there was no longer any need. She now recognized that her husband lived within her heart and that she could honor their love by continuing to live with faith and devotion.

Her transformation reveals the healing power of spiritual insight. Tulsidas did not ask her to forget her husband or deny her grief. Instead, he guided her toward a deeper understanding of love—one that survives separation and physical death. What had begun as unbearable sorrow became an enduring inner union, sustained by memory, devotion, and awareness of the divine.
outputs.L5:
Tulsidas sat beside the Ganges at dawn, listening to the river flow like an ancient hymn. In its silver currents, he found the rhythm of devotion and the quiet strength to shape sacred stories into words ordinary people could understand.

She came to the river each morning carrying a small lamp and a handful of flowers. Though she had never met the poet, his verses lived in her memory. As she set the lamp upon the water, she whispered a prayer and watched it drift beneath the brightening sky. For her, the Ganges was more than a river, and Tulsidas was more than a poet: both were bridges between human longing and the divine.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short spiritual parable about Tulsidas helping a grieving widow discover that her husband lives on in her heart.
counterfactuals.output:
A grieving widow came to Tulsidas and said, “My husband is gone, and with him all light has left my life.”

Tulsidas gave her an unlit lamp and asked, “Where is its flame?”

“There is none,” she replied.

He struck a spark and lit the wick. “Was the flame hiding inside the lamp?”

“No,” she said. “It arose when fire touched it.”

Tulsidas smiled. “So it is with love. Your husband’s body was the lamp, but the love you shared is the flame. The lamp may pass from sight, yet the flame can kindle courage, kindness, and remembrance within you.”

The widow held the lamp close. In its gentle light, she understood that grief was not proof that love had ended, but proof that it still burned.

From that day on, whenever she missed her husband, she lit a lamp and offered some kindness in his memory. And thus he lived on—not as a shadow behind her, but as a light within her heart.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Retell an Indian folktale in which a widow preparing to follow her dead husband is guided by the poet Tulsidas toward divine love.
counterfactuals.output:
### The Widow and Tulsidas

In an old tale from northern India, a young widow walked toward the riverbank where her husband’s funeral pyre had been raised. Overcome by grief, she had resolved to enter the flames, believing that life without him held no meaning.

On the road she met Tulsidas, the poet-saint devoted to Lord Rama. Seeing her funeral garments and sorrowful face, he asked where she was going.

“To follow my husband,” she replied. “All my love belonged to him. Now that he is gone, what remains for me?”

Tulsidas looked at her with compassion.

“If love can make you surrender even your life,” he said, “then do not offer it to the fire. Offer it to the Eternal One. The body you mourn was mortal, as all bodies are, but the divine presence within him has not died. Seek that presence in Rama, and you will find your husband, yourself, and all beings embraced in one boundless love.”

The widow protested, “But how can I live with such pain?”

“Let every tear become a prayer,” Tulsidas answered. “Let every memory become the name of Rama. True devotion does not demand that you destroy yourself. It asks you to let selfishness, despair, and ignorance burn away.”

His words entered her heart. She turned back from the pyre and began a new life devoted to prayer and service. In time, her grief softened into compassion, and she became known for comforting others who had suffered loss.

Thus, the tale says, she did follow her husband—not into the flames, but toward the divine love dwelling beyond death.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a concise, dialogue-rich story set beside the Ganges, featuring Tulsidas, a funeral pyre, and a widow who ultimately finds her lost husband within herself.
counterfactuals.output:
At dusk beside the Ganges, a widow knelt before her husband’s funeral pyre.

“Wait,” said Tulsidas, approaching through the smoke.

“What remains to wait for?” she asked. “My husband is gone.”

“Where did you lose him?”

She pointed to the shrouded body. “There.”

Tulsidas touched his chest. “Was he only this?”

“No. He was his laughter, his kindness, his anger.”

“And where are those now?”

“In my memory.”

“Look deeper.”

The pyre cracked. Sparks rose like fireflies over the river.

The widow closed her eyes. She heard his laughter in her breath, felt his kindness in her hands, even his anger in the fierce beat of her heart.

“He is here,” she whispered.

Tulsidas nodded. “Love does not keep the body. It remakes the one who loves.”

She lit the pyre. Flames lifted toward the darkening sky.

“Farewell,” she said, touching her heart, “and welcome home.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you narrate the tale of Tulsidas promising a bereaved woman that she will find her husband before the month ends?
counterfactuals.output:
According to a popular devotional legend, a woman once came to Tulsidas overwhelmed with grief. Her husband had disappeared, and after long, fruitless searching she had begun to fear that he was dead. Falling at the poet-saint’s feet, she begged him for some word of hope.

Tulsidas, absorbed in devotion to Rama, told her calmly, “Do not surrender to despair. Before this month has ended, you will find your husband.”

She accepted the assurance as a blessing and returned home. The days passed, but there was still no news. Then, near the close of the month, word came that a man had been found alive after misfortune had delayed or stranded him far from home. The woman hurried to the place and discovered that it was indeed her husband. The couple were reunited before the month ended, just as Tulsidas had promised.

When people praised Tulsidas for foreseeing the event, he disclaimed any personal power. Whatever had happened, he said, was due not to him but to the grace of Rama, whose name sustains those who place their trust in it.

The details vary among oral retellings. In a better-known related legend, Tulsidas blesses a newly bereaved woman with the words “May you remain married,” and her dead husband is restored to life through the chanting of Rama’s name. Both stories express the same devotional idea: Tulsidas’s words carried power only because of his complete faith in Rama.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an old-fashioned mystical story about grief and spiritual awakening, ending with the line, “In my heart is my lord, one with me.”
counterfactuals.output:
In the elder days, when the hills were clothed in forests and the roads between villages were little more than ribbons of mud, there lived beside a dark mere a woman named Elspeth.

She had once shared her cottage with her husband, Rowan, a quiet man who mended clocks and sang to himself as he worked. Yet in the winter of their seventh year together, a fever came down from the northern moors. Before the first thaw, Rowan was laid beneath the yew tree in the churchyard.

Thereafter, Elspeth moved through her days as one wandering in a ruined house. She covered the mirrors, let the fire burn low, and kept Rowan’s cup upon the table, though dust gathered in it. Neighbours brought broth and kind words, but she heard them dimly, as though they spoke from the far side of deep water.

One evening, on the first anniversary of Rowan’s death, a storm rose over the mere. The wind shook the shutters, and from the chimney came a sound like mournful chanting. Unable to bear the cottage’s emptiness, Elspeth wrapped herself in a woollen cloak and went out into the rain.

She walked without purpose until she reached the old stone chapel in the forest, long abandoned by priest and pilgrim. Its roof had fallen in, and ivy coiled about the broken altar. Yet as Elspeth entered, she saw a small lamp burning there.

Beside it sat an ancient woman in a robe the colour of ashes.

“Whom do you seek?” asked the stranger.

“My husband,” Elspeth replied.

“Where have you sought him?”

“In dreams, in memories, in every shadow by the door.”

“And have you sought him in your grief?”

Elspeth grew angry. “Grief is the gate that shut him from me.”

“Nay,” said the old woman. “Grief is the gate. Thou hast only feared to open it.”

At these words, the lamp went out.

Darkness covered the chapel, and Elspeth heard the storm recede until there remained no sound but the beating of her heart. Then the stones beneath her feet seemed to vanish. She felt herself falling through a measureless night.

In that night she saw all she had lost: Rowan laughing beneath an apple tree; Rowan sleeping by the hearth; Rowan turning once upon the winter road to lift his hand in farewell. Each vision pierced her, and she cried out until her voice failed.

But still she fell.

At last she ceased to struggle. She opened her arms to the darkness and said, “Take what remains of me.”

Then a wonder came to pass.

The darkness did not take her. It entered her sorrow and made it vast. Her grief widened beyond herself, beyond Rowan, beyond the little cottage and the lonely grave. She felt within it every mother who had buried a child, every sailor who had vanished at sea, every exile who had looked homeward and found no road. Their tears became hers, and hers became theirs.

Yet beneath those innumerable sorrows moved a hidden current—warm, golden, and without end.

Elspeth saw that love was not a chain binding one soul to another, but a flame passing through all souls. Forms perished; names faded; hands parted. But the flame was neither born nor buried. It dwelt in the seed beneath the frost, in the stars beyond the clouds, in the living and the dead alike.

When she opened her eyes, dawn had come.

The ruined chapel was empty. No lamp stood upon the altar, nor was there any sign that another traveller had sheltered there. Elspeth returned through the dripping wood, and every branch shone as though newly made.

She did not forget Rowan. She tended his grave and sometimes wept beside it. But her tears were no longer a prison. They were rain upon holy ground.

In the years that followed, sorrowing folk came to her cottage by the mere. Elspeth gave them bread, listened to their tales, and asked no payment. When they begged her to speak of death, she told them that the beloved does not dwell behind us, imprisoned in memory, but within the boundless life from which no soul is ever severed.

And when Elspeth herself grew old, she went one spring morning to the yew tree and lay down among the bluebells. The bells of the village sounded across the fields, though no hand was pulling the rope.

She closed her eyes, smiling as one who beholds a long-expected traveller, and whispered, “In my heart is my lord, one with me.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
